title: Cybersecurity Analyst
subtitle: 20 questions across threat intel, vulnerability management, SIEM, incident response, and forensics

gradeLabels.f: F-RANK -- Back to the Alert Queue

questions.q: In the Cyber Kill Chain, which stage immediately follows Weaponization?
questions.note: The order is: Recon > Weaponization > Delivery > Exploitation > Installation > C2 > Actions.

explain.correct: Delivery is the third stage -- the attacker transmits the weapon to the target (e.g., phishing email, USB drop).
wrong: Exploitation comes AFTER Delivery -- the weapon must reach the target before it can trigger.
Installation is two stages after Delivery; the payload must be delivered and executed first.
Reconnaissance is the very FIRST stage, occurring before Weaponization.

questions.q: Which of the following is the correct set of vertices in the Diamond Model of intrusion analysis?
questions.note: Diamond Model: Adversary -- Capability -- Infrastructure -- Victim form the four vertices.

explain.correct: Adversary, Capability, Infrastructure, Victim are the four nodes; edges represent relationships between them.
wrong: Tactic, Technique, Procedure, Tool (TTPs + Tool) describe MITRE ATT&CK behaviors, not Diamond Model vertices.
Host, Network, User, Data is not a recognized threat-intel framework vertex set.
Threat, Vulnerability, Risk, Control belongs to risk management vocabulary, not the Diamond Model.

questions.q: An analyst wants to share threat intelligence in a machine-readable format with partner organizations. Which standard describes the DATA FORMAT used to represent this intelligence?
questions.note: STIX (Structured Threat Information eXpression) is the data format; TAXII is the transport protocol.

explain.correct: STIX defines the schema and format for expressing cyber threat intelligence objects such as indicators, malware, and campaigns.
wrong: OpenIOC is a Mandiant/FireEye indicator format but is not the dominant machine-readable CTI standard paired with TAXII.
YARA is a pattern-matching rule language used to identify malware samples, not a structured intelligence sharing format.
TAXII (Trusted Automated eXchange of Intelligence Information) is the TRANSPORT protocol that carries STIX content -- not the format itself.

questions.q: A vulnerability scanner reports a CVSS v3.1 base score of 9.8. Which severity band does this score fall into?

explain.correct: 9.8 falls in the 9.0-10.0 range, which is Critical -- the highest severity band.
wrong: High covers 7.0-8.9. A score of 9.8 exceeds the High ceiling and lands in Critical.
Medium covers 4.0-6.9. 9.8 is nearly 5 points above the Medium ceiling.
Low covers 0.1-3.9. 9.8 is far outside this band.

questions.q: Windows Security Event ID 4625 is logged when which action occurs?
options: A user fails to log on
A user account is locked out
questions.note: 4625 = failed logon attempt. 4624 = successful logon. 4688 = new process creation.

explain.correct: Event ID 4625 records every failed interactive or network logon attempt, including the reason code (e.g., wrong password, disabled account).
wrong: New process creation is Event ID 4688, not 4625.
Scheduled task registration is Event ID 4698, not 4625.
Account lockout generates Event ID 4740, not 4625 -- though 4625 events can precede a lockout.

questions.q: In MITRE ATT&CK, what is the difference between a TACTIC and a TECHNIQUE?
options: A tactic is a sub-step of a technique
A tactic and technique are synonymous terms
A tactic is the specific tool used; a technique is the adversary goal
A tactic is the adversary goal; a technique is how they achieve it
questions.note: ATT&CK Tactics = WHY (goal); Techniques = HOW (method). Sub-techniques add further granularity.

explain.correct: Tactics represent the adversary's tactical objective (e.g., Persistence, Exfiltration). Techniques describe the specific method used to accomplish that objective (e.g., Registry Run Keys for Persistence).
wrong: Sub-techniques are sub-steps of techniques, not tactics. Tactics sit ABOVE techniques in the hierarchy.
The two terms are distinct and non-interchangeable in the ATT&CK framework.
This reversal is a common confusion -- tactics are goals, not tools. Specific tools are tracked in the Software category.

questions.q: Which CVSS v3.1 base metric asks whether the vulnerability can be exploited without any authentication or privileges on the target system?
questions.note: Privileges Required (PR) measures what access level the attacker needs before exploiting the vulnerability.

explain.correct: Privileges Required is rated None, Low, or High -- a value of None means no authentication is needed, which increases the base score significantly.
wrong: Attack Complexity (AC) measures whether conditions beyond the attacker's control must exist -- not the privilege level required.
Scope (S) indicates whether the impact extends beyond the vulnerable component to other components.
User Interaction (UI) measures whether a human must take an action (e.g., click a link) for the exploit to succeed.

questions.q: Which identifier system classifies a CATEGORY of software weakness (e.g., buffer overflow, SQL injection) rather than a specific vulnerability instance?
questions.note: CWE = weakness category; CVE = specific vulnerability instance; CPE = product naming; EPSS = exploitation probability.

explain.correct: Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) catalogs generic weakness types such as CWE-89 (SQL Injection) or CWE-121 (Stack-based Buffer Overflow).
wrong: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) identifies a SPECIFIC, unique vulnerability in a specific product version -- not a category.
Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) estimates the probability that a CVE will be exploited in the wild within 30 days.
Common Platform Enumeration (CPE) is a structured naming scheme for hardware and software products.

questions.q: During a forensic investigation, an analyst must collect volatile data from a live Windows system. According to the order of volatility, which source should be collected FIRST?
questions.note: Order of volatility (most to least): CPU cache/registers > RAM > network state/processes > disk > archival media.

explain.correct: RAM is the most volatile storage beyond CPU registers -- it is lost the moment the system is powered off or rebooted. It must be captured before anything else.
wrong: Hard disk data persists after power-off; it is far less volatile than RAM and is collected later in the order.
Log files reside on disk and are non-volatile relative to RAM; they can be collected after memory.
Archival backup tapes are the LEAST volatile source and are collected last in the order.

questions.q: A SOC analyst observes that a compromised endpoint is making outbound HTTPS connections to the same external IP every 300 seconds with near-zero variance. This traffic pattern is BEST described as:
questions.note: Beaconing = periodic, regular-interval callbacks from malware to a C2 server.

explain.correct: Beaconing is the characteristic pattern of malware checking in with its C2 at predictable, repeating intervals -- the regularity is the key tell.
wrong: DNS tunneling hides data INSIDE DNS query/response payloads for exfiltration -- it does not specifically describe timed HTTPS callbacks.
Fast flux rapidly rotates the IP addresses associated with a domain to evade blocklisting; it is a DNS evasion technique, not a callback timing pattern.
DGA malware generates many pseudo-random domain names algorithmically to find an active C2; the timing of HTTPS calls at fixed intervals is beaconing, not DGA activity.

questions.q: Which email authentication mechanism adds a cryptographic SIGNATURE to message headers so the receiving mail server can verify the message was not altered in transit?
questions.note: DKIM signs the message; SPF lists authorized sending IPs; DMARC enforces policy and reporting on top of both.

explain.correct: DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) attaches a public-key cryptographic signature in a message header; the receiving server retrieves the public key from DNS to verify integrity and sender authenticity.
wrong: SPF (Sender Policy Framework) publishes a list of authorized sending IP addresses in a DNS TXT record -- it verifies the sending server, not message content integrity.

DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance) builds on SPF and DKIM by specifying a policy (none/quarantine/reject) and a reporting address; it does not itself perform the cryptographic signing.
An MX record designates the mail server for a domain; it has no authentication or signing function.

questions.q: A threat hunter queries SIEM logs and finds hundreds of short-lived domain names queried in rapid succession from a single host, each resolving to a different IP, none matching known blocklists. This BEST indicates:
questions.note: DGA malware generates many algorithmically derived domain names; most fail to resolve, a few succeed -- producing this query storm pattern.

explain.correct: Domain Generation Algorithms produce long lists of pseudo-random domains; the malware queries each until one resolves to the active C2. The high query volume with random-looking names is the signature DGA indicator.
wrong: SPF failures relate to email sender authorization checks, not DNS query behavior from an endpoint.
Beaconing features regular interval callbacks to a CONSISTENT destination -- not hundreds of distinct domain queries.
Fast flux involves rotating IPs behind a SINGLE domain with short TTLs; DGA involves MANY distinct generated domains, not one domain with many IPs.

questions.q: What is the CORRECT order of the four phases in the NIST SP 800-61 incident response lifecycle?
options: Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication, and Recovery; Post-Incident Activity
Detection and Analysis; Preparation; Containment, Eradication, and Recovery; Post-Incident Activity
Preparation; Post-Incident Activity; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication, and Recovery
Preparation; Containment, Eradication, and Recovery; Detection and Analysis; Post-Incident Activity
questions.note: NIST 800-61 phases: 1-Preparation, 2-Detection and Analysis, 3-Containment/Eradication/Recovery, 4-Post-Incident Activity.

explain.correct: Preparation comes first (tools, plans, training); Detection and Analysis second (identify and scope the incident); Containment, Eradication, and Recovery third (stop, remove, restore); Post-Incident Activity last (lessons learned, documentation).
wrong: Preparation cannot follow Detection -- Preparation is the foundational phase that must occur BEFORE any incident.
Post-Incident Activity is out of position here -- lessons-learned activities happen AFTER recovery, not before Detection.
This sequence incorrectly places Containment before Detection -- you cannot contain an incident you have not yet detected and analyzed.

questions.q: During incident response, a SOC team isolates a single compromised workstation from the network while preserving its running state to allow further analysis. This action BEST represents:
questions.note: Short-term containment = immediate isolation to stop spread. Long-term = sustained measures that allow some operations to continue.

explain.correct: Short-term containment involves immediate actions -- such as pulling a network cable or disabling a switch port -- to prevent spread while preserving evidence for analysis.
wrong: Eradication is the act of removing the root cause (malware, backdoor, compromised credentials) AFTER the system is contained.
Long-term containment involves more sustainable measures (e.g., placing the system in a monitored segment) that can remain in place for days while a fix is prepared.
Post-incident activity is the final phase covering lessons-learned meetings, report writing, and control improvement -- not active response steps.

questions.q: A digital forensics analyst creates an exact replica of a suspect hard drive using 'dd' and then runs SHA-256 on both the source and the copy. The hashes match. What has this process PRIMARILY established?
options: That the drive has no hidden partitions
Chain of custody for the evidence
A forensic image verified by hash integrity
questions.note: A forensic image is a bitwise copy + cryptographic hash verification. The hash proves the copy is identical to the source.

explain.correct: A forensic image created by 'dd' is a bitwise (bit-for-bit) copy. Matching SHA-256 hashes on the source and copy prove the copy is identical -- this is the foundation of forensic image integrity verification.
wrong: Matching hashes confirm the entire bit-for-bit copy is identical; they do not scan for hidden partitions (tools like 'fdisk' or 'mmls' would be used for that).
Volatility order compliance refers to the sequence in which volatile data sources are collected (RAM before disk) -- it is unrelated to hash verification of a disk image.
Chain of custody is a documented record of who handled evidence, when, and what actions were taken. A hash alone does not establish chain of custody -- documentation and handling records do.

questions.q: An Nmap scan is run with the flag '-sS'. What type of scan does this flag invoke?
questions.note: Nmap -sS = SYN scan (sends SYN, reads SYN-ACK/RST, never completes the handshake). -sV = version detection. -O = OS detection.

explain.correct: -sS performs a TCP SYN scan: Nmap sends a SYN packet and reads the response (SYN-ACK = open, RST = closed) without completing the three-way handshake, making it stealthier than a full connect scan.
wrong: A full TCP connect scan (-sT) completes the entire three-way handshake; -sS deliberately avoids this.
Service and version detection is -sV, which sends additional probes after finding open ports to identify the running service and its version.
OS fingerprinting is -O, which analyzes TCP/IP stack behavior to guess the operating system.

questions.q: A credentialed vulnerability scan is run against a web server compared to an uncredentialed scan of the same target. Which statement BEST describes the expected difference in results?
options: The uncredentialed scan finds more vulnerabilities and has fewer false positives
Both scans produce identical results if run against the same host
Credentialed scans can only be run internally; uncredentialed scans only externally
The credentialed scan finds more vulnerabilities and has fewer false positives
questions.note: Credentialed scans authenticate to the target and inspect patch levels, configurations, and installed software -- yielding more findings with higher accuracy.

explain.correct: Credentialed scans log into the target system and inspect it from the inside (registry keys, installed packages, patch levels), finding vulnerabilities that are invisible to external probing and generating fewer false positives.
wrong: Uncredentialed (unauthenticated) scans infer vulnerabilities from externally visible service banners and behavior -- they miss internal weaknesses and generate more false positives because they cannot confirm patch levels.
The two scan types produce significantly different result sets; credentialed scans consistently surface more findings.
Either scan type can be run from internal or external network positions; authentication is independent of network location.

questions.q: A malware sample adds an entry under 'HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run'. What threat behavior does this MOST directly represent?
questions.note: Registry Run keys cause malware to re-execute at each user logon -- a classic Windows persistence mechanism mapped to MITRE ATT&CK T1547.001.

explain.correct: Adding a value to a Windows Run key ensures the payload executes automatically at each logon without requiring re-exploitation. This is the defining behavior of the Persistence tactic in ATT&CK.
wrong: Privilege escalation involves gaining higher-level access (e.g., from user to SYSTEM). A Run key entry does not elevate privileges.
Lateral movement involves moving between systems within the network. A Run key entry is local to the compromised host.
Defense evasion involves hiding malicious activity (e.g., disabling logging, process injection). A Run key is a persistence mechanism, though it may be combined with evasion techniques.

questions.q: What distinguishes a SECURITY INCIDENT from a SECURITY EVENT in SOC operations?
options: An event is any observable occurrence; an incident is a violation or imminent threat to security policy
Events are generated only by network devices; incidents are generated only by endpoints
An event requires immediate escalation; an incident does not
An incident is any observable occurrence; an event is a confirmed policy violation
questions.note: Event = any observable occurrence. Incident = a confirmed violation or imminent threat requiring a response. Not every event becomes an incident.

explain.correct: A security event is any observable occurrence in a system or network (e.g., a failed login). A security incident is an event or series of events that violates -- or imminently threatens to violate -- security policy, requiring a formal response.
wrong: Both events and incidents can originate from any device type -- network, endpoint, application, or cloud -- regardless of source.
Events do not inherently require immediate escalation; most events are benign. It is incidents that trigger escalation and the IR lifecycle.
This definition has the two terms reversed. Incidents are violations; events are generic observable occurrences.

questions.q: Which statement CORRECTLY describes the role of DMARC in email authentication?
options: DMARC publishes a list of IP addresses authorized to send mail for the domain
DMARC defines a policy for how receivers handle SPF/DKIM failures and requests reporting
DMARC encrypts the email in transit between mail servers
DMARC cryptographically signs the email body to prevent tampering
questions.note: DMARC instructs receivers what to do when SPF or DKIM checks fail (none/quarantine/reject) and provides a reporting address for aggregate data.

explain.correct: DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance) layers on top of SPF and DKIM. Its policy tag (p=) tells receiving servers to do nothing, quarantine, or reject messages that fail alignment. The 'rua' tag requests aggregate failure reports sent back to the domain owner.
wrong: Publishing a list of authorized sending IP addresses in DNS is the function of SPF, not DMARC.
Encrypting email in transit is the function of TLS (STARTTLS or SMTPS). DMARC does not provide encryption.
Cryptographic signing of the message is the role of DKIM, not DMARC. DMARC references the DKIM result rather than performing signing itself.
